title: Naso: the nazirite (Numbers 6:1–21)
hookLine: a person may vow to give up wine and haircuts for a season

lines: DRY JANUARY. NO SUGAR TILL THE WEDDING.
A VOW WITH AN END DATE.
cards: Dry January. A month without social media. No sugar until the wedding.
A beard grown out for a cause. A fixed-term vow is a familiar idea: something hard, something visible, with an end date circled on the calendar.
The Torah has one too, with rules, a start, an end, and a ceremony to close it. You'd spot this person in a crowd. Long hair, never cut for the whole season.
A cup of water where everyone else is drinking wine. Numbers chapter six calls them the nazirite.

teach.b: The chapter opens: when either a man or a woman makes a special vow to be a nazir, set apart for the LORD. Man or woman: anyone could take this vow. Then three rules.

teach.h: NO WINE, NO RAZOR, NO DEAD.
teach.b: No wine and nothing from grapes, not even raisins, seeds or skins. No razor on the head; the hair grows wild for the whole term. And no contact with the dead, not even at the funeral of one's own parents.

The verse says the nazirite is holy to the LORD for all those days. Nazir means one set apart. The verse calls what's on the nazirite's head the nezer, the consecration, a word that elsewhere means a crown.

teach.h: THIRTY DAYS, THEN THE HAIR BURNS.
teach.b: If no length is named, the Mishnah says the vow runs thirty days. At the end the nazirite brings offerings, shaves the head at the sanctuary door, and puts the hair on the fire.
Then, the verse says, they may drink wine again. The vow was always for a season. Here's where it gets interesting.
One of those closing offerings is a sin offering.
Why would someone who gave things up for God need atonement? The Talmud keeps two answers side by side. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says: because they denied themselves wine, which God made good.
If refusing wine needs atonement, how much more refusing everything. Other sages point to the verse itself: the nazirite shall be holy. Both views stay on the page.
A vow can lift you, and it can also curdle into scorn for ordinary life. The Torah gives it an end date.

how: The nazirite vow, described in Numbers 6 and the Mishnah's tractate Nazir, depended on the Temple's offerings and is not practiced today; Jewish teachers still discuss it as a model, and a warning, about holy self-denial.

a mourner who lets the hair grow long

games.q: the nazirite's term ends. among the offerings is a sin offering. why, according to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar?
o: for denying themselves wine, which God made good.
games.why: he argues that refusing a good thing needs atonement. other sages point to the verse: the nazirite shall be holy. both views stay in the Talmud.

practice: Look for something that's become automatic, the second coffee, scrolling in bed, complaining about traffic, and picture a week without it: not forever, seven days, with an end you can see.
Notice whether the giving up feels like a crown or a fence. Either is worth knowing.
